newsitem.title: GERMANY: Jochimsen-EMU timetable must not outweigh criteria.
newsitem.headline: Jochimsen-EMU timetable must not outweigh criteria.

text.p: Bundesbank council member Reimut Jochimsen was quoted on Thursday as saying it would be wrong to give the timetable for European monetary union precedence over meeting the Maastricht treaty membership criteria.
He was responding to France's admission that its budget deficit will probably exceed in 1997 the Maastricht target limiting the shortfall to three percent of gross domestic product.

Asked whether the expected French deficit overshoot meant that France should not participate in the launch of the single currency, Jochimsen was quoted in the German magazine WirtschaftsWoche as saying:
"...a softening endangers the stability of the euro. The Treaty has set the upper deficit limit at three percent (of GDP), politicians have solemnly pledged adherence to it."
"Even if France or Germany did not pass the test it would be wrong to give the timetable absolute priority over the criteria." It was irresponsible to adopt the maxim "Now at any price," he added.

French finance minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn said last week that France's deficit would probably exceed three percent of gross domestic product in 1997, the key year for deciding which EU nations qualify for the euro from the start.
He reinforced that prediction on Thursday, saying France's public deficit could be "significantly higher" than 3.0 percent.

Asked if it made sense to start monetary union without France said, Jochimsen said that if there was any doubt, and if the timetable for the launch was regarded as sacrosanct, the single currency should start with a small group of members.

Referring to French calls for a political counterweight to the European Central Bank, Jochimsen said the Maastricht Treaty stated that the bank must be independent and not subject to politicians' instructions.
"One cannot introduce a common currency if there is disagreement on these principles."
He added he was convinced the Bundesbank would be asked for its opinion in 1998 on whether Germany had met the Maastricht criteria as strictly as required by both houses of the federal parliament.
